title: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
summary: How learned models replace hand-tuned systems policies: learned indexes that predict key positions, LRB's learned CDN eviction, Decima's RL cluster scheduler, and the guardrails that keep them correct.
outcomes: Compute the gap between LRU and Belady's MIN on a trace and explain why MIN is only a yardstick
Build a tiny learned index by hand, derive its error window and explain how a recursive model index shrinks it
Explain how LRB uses the Belady boundary, sampled candidates and a GBM to approximate relaxed Belady
Explain Decima's graph embeddings, action encoding, JCT reward and the training tricks that make RL work
Choose guardrails, inference budgets and retraining plans that keep a learned policy safe under drift

lessons.title: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN

blocks.md:
Every system is full of small decision policies: which page a buffer pool evicts, which job gets the next free executor, where in a sorted array a key probably lives. You met several of these in the buffer pool course (LRU, CLOCK, LRU-K, 2Q). Each one is a **heuristic**: a fixed rule, written by a person, tuned so it works acceptably on many workloads.

**ML for systems** replaces such a rule with a model trained on the workload the system actually sees. This course follows three landmark designs: learned indexes (Kraska et al., 2018), learned CDN caching with LRB (Song et al., NSDI 2020) and learned cluster scheduling with Decima (Mao et al., SIGCOMM 2019).

To know how much a better policy could gain, we need a yardstick. For caching it is **Belady's MIN**: on a miss with a full cache, evict the object whose next request is furthest in the future. With equal-sized objects it produces the fewest misses of any policy. It needs the future, so no real cache can run it; it is computed offline on a recorded trace and used as an upper bound on what is achievable.

blocks.prompt: A cache holds 3 objects. The request trace is A B C D A B E A B C D E (12 requests). How many hits does LRU get, and how many does MIN get?
blocks.reveal: LRU gets **2 hits** and MIN gets **5 hits** (10 versus 7 misses). The loop A B C D is one object larger than the cache, so LRU always evicts exactly the object that is about to come back. MIN looks ahead and sacrifices the object needed last. Step through the figure below to see every eviction.

blocks.title: LRU versus Belady's MIN on a 3-slot cache

scenes.caption: After the first three requests both caches hold A, B, C (3 compulsory misses each). The LRU row is ordered from least to most recently used.
D misses. LRU evicts A, the oldest. MIN checks next uses: A in 1 request, B in 2, C in 6, so it evicts C.
A and B return. LRU just evicted A and then evicts B to make room: 2 more misses. MIN still holds both: 2 hits.
E misses for both. Both evict D here (MIN: A is needed in 1, B in 2, D in 4). Then A and B hit in both caches. Hits so far: LRU 2, MIN 4.
C, D, E. LRU misses all three. MIN evicts A then C (never requested again) and keeps E, which hits at the end. Final: LRU 2 hits, MIN 5 hits.

blocks.md: MIN is not a policy you can deploy, and it is not what learned caches try to predict exactly. It is a **yardstick**. Its value is telling you how big the gap is. On six production CDN traces with a 1 TB cache, the LRB authors measured a 25 to 40% gap in byte miss ratio between MIN and the best online policies they tested.

A heuristic is a guess about the future written down once. LRU guesses that recently used means soon used again. That guess fails on loops slightly larger than the cache, on scans, and on the many CDN objects that are requested only once. A model trained on the system's own history can learn which signals actually predict the future *for this workload*.

The catch is that a model makes mistakes, costs CPU time on a path that used to cost a few instructions, and was trained on yesterday's traffic. Every successful design in this course pairs the model with structure that bounds the damage.

blocks.title: The pattern: a model inside a guarded decision point

scenes.caption: Today: a fixed rule (LRU, FIFO, a B-tree traversal) turns each request into an action. It is cheap and predictable but never adapts.
Learned version: describe the request with features, ask a trained model, act on its prediction.
The guard is what makes it safe: a bounded search window, a small sample of legal choices, or a fallback rule. A wrong prediction then costs time, not correctness.
Outcomes are logged and used to retrain, because the workload drifts. Training cost and data collection are part of the design, not an afterthought.

blocks.md: In all three systems the model chooses among **correct** options: any position inside a verified error window, any cached object to evict, any runnable stage to schedule. A bad model can make the system slower, but the surrounding structure keeps it correct.

blocks.question: A 3-slot cache holds X, Y and Z. Their next requests are: X in 7 requests, Y never, Z in 2 requests. A miss for W arrives. What does Belady's MIN evict?
options: Z, because it was used least recently
X, because it is needed later than Z
Y, because it is never requested again
W is not admitted, because MIN only evicts on hits
blocks.explain: MIN evicts the object whose next request is furthest away, and never counts as furthest of all. Recency (option one) is LRU's rule, not MIN's. X is a reasonable second choice but loses to Y.

blocks.question: Why do learned-systems papers compare against Belady's MIN even though nobody can deploy it?
options: It shows how much room is left above current heuristics, so you know whether a better policy can pay off
It is the policy the model is trained to reproduce exactly, decision for decision
It is the fastest policy to compute online
blocks.explain: MIN needs future requests, so it is only computable offline. It bounds what any online policy can achieve, which turns 'LRU gets 2 hits' into 'LRU gets 2 of a possible 5'. As lesson 3 shows, LRB deliberately does not try to match MIN decision for decision.

lessons.title: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives

blocks.md:
Take a read-only, in-memory array of records sorted by key. A B-tree over it maps a lookup key to a page, then you search inside that page. Kraska et al. point out that this *is* a model: it maps a key to a position with a **min error** of 0 and a **max error** of the page size, and it guarantees the key is inside that range if it exists.

So any function that maps key to position, plus a guaranteed error range, can do the B-tree's job. If the keys are 1,000,000 to 1,999,999, the model `position = key - 1000000` is perfect: one subtraction, no tree walk.

A position in a sorted array is just the number of keys smaller than the lookup key. That is the **cumulative distribution function** (CDF) of the keys, scaled by the number of keys $N$. Learning an index therefore means learning the data distribution:

blocks.caption: F is the estimated CDF, P(X <= key), and N is the number of keys. A B-tree learns F as a regression tree; a linear model learns it by least squares.

blocks.md: Our running example has $N = 12$ sorted keys: 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 12, 17, 25, 38, 52, 70, 95. They are dense at the start and sparse at the end, like many real key sets (timestamps with bursts, IDs with gaps). A least-squares line through (key, position) gives $p \approx 0.1085 \cdot \text{key} + 2.48$.

blocks.title: 12 keys, one linear model, then a 2-stage model

scenes.caption: Dots are the true (key, position) pairs: the empirical CDF scaled by N. The single line follows the overall shape but misses the dense head and sparse tail.
Rounded to integers, the line's errors (true minus predicted) range from -3 (key 2) to +2 (keys 17 and 25). Those two numbers are all the index must store to guarantee correctness.
A 2-stage recursive model index: the top line only picks one of 3 leaf lines, each fit to its own slice of keys. The leaf errors shrink to the range 0 to +1.

blocks.md: A lookup runs the model, then searches only the window between prediction plus min error and prediction plus max error. These bounds are computed by running the model over every stored key after training, exactly as the paper describes.

blocks.title: Looking up key 38: the error window decides the search cost

scenes.caption: Single model: 0.1085 times 38 plus 2.48 is 6.60, rounded to 7. With stored errors -3 to +2, the key must be in positions 4 to 9: a window of 6 instead of 12.
Binary search inside the window needs at most 3 probes (6 slots) instead of 4 for the whole array. Key 38 is at position 8, one past the prediction.
2-stage model: the top line predicts 6.60, which routes to leaf 1 of 3 (floor of 3 times 6.60 over 12 is 1). Leaf 1 was fit only to keys 17, 25, 38 and predicts 8.06, rounded to 8.
Leaf 1 has zero error on its keys, so the window is the single slot 8: one comparison confirms the hit. Better models buy smaller windows, which buy fewer cache misses.

blocks.prompt: Why not just train one bigger model (say a neural net) to predict every position within plus or minus 1, instead of stacking small models?
blocks.reveal: The paper found that the overall shape of a CDF is easy to learn, but the last mile is hard: zoomed in, real key sets are irregular, and squeezing the error from thousands down to hundreds with one model costs a lot of space and CPU. Splitting the key space, like a B-tree does, lets each small leaf model learn a nearly straight piece. In the paper's 2-stage experiments simple linear models worked best for the leaves.

blocks.md: The **recursive model index** (RMI) is a hierarchy of models. Stage 0 sees the key and outputs a number used only to pick a model in stage 1, and so on until the last stage predicts the position. Model $k$ of stage $\ell$ is trained only on the keys routed to it:

blocks.caption: Stage l has M_l models. The previous stage's prediction, scaled to M_l buckets, selects which model handles key x. Each stage is trained in turn on squared error.

blocks.title: RMI lookup for key 38, line by line
blocks.code:
def lookup(key):
    p0 = a0 * key + b0              # stage 0
    j = floor(M * p0 / N)           # route to a leaf
    j = min(max(j, 0), M - 1)
    a, b, lo_err, hi_err = leaf[j]
    p = round(a * key + b)          # leaf prediction
    lo = max(p + lo_err, 0)
    hi = min(p + hi_err, N - 1)
    return lower_bound(keys, key, lo, hi)

scenes.caption: Stage 0 is the single line from before. Its output is not used as a position, only for routing.
With M = 3 leaves and N = 12 keys, 3 times 6.603 divided by 12 is 1.65, so leaf 1 handles this key.
Leaf 1 stores its line and the worst under- and over-prediction it made on its own keys.
0.0935 times 38 plus 4.507 is 8.06, rounded to 8.
The window is clamped to the array. Here it is one slot, so the final search is a single comparison.

blocks.md:
Why can this beat a B-tree? The paper's back-of-envelope: a B-tree over 100M records with 100 keys per page needs $\log_{100} 10^8 = 4$ node visits, and binary search inside one page takes roughly 50 cycles. A CPU can do 8 to 16 SIMD operations per cycle, so a model wins if it narrows the range more than 100-fold per 400 arithmetic operations, and each avoided cache miss (50 to 100 cycles) buys even more room.

The abstract reports learned indexes up to 70% faster than cache-optimized B-trees while using an order of magnitude less memory on several real datasets.

Model execution must be nearly free. The paper's first attempt ran a 2-layer, 32-neuron net through TensorFlow from Python: about 80,000 ns per prediction, versus about 300 ns for a whole B-tree traversal. Their Learning Index Framework instead extracts the trained weights and generates small C++ index code, never calling TensorFlow at lookup time.

Three details keep the index honest:

- **Hybrid fallback.** After training, any leaf whose max absolute error exceeds a threshold is replaced by a B-tree. The worst case is then roughly a B-tree, not a bad model.
- **Absent keys.** The stored error bounds hold for keys in the set. For a key not in the set, a non-monotonic model can point to the wrong window; the fixes are monotonic models or exponential search outward from the prediction.
- **Inserts.** The paper targets read-mostly data. Its suggested route for writes is a delta index: buffer inserts, then periodically merge them and retrain. Later designs such as the PGM-index add provable bounds on query cost.

blocks.question: A single-model learned index stores min error -3 and max error +2. What is the worst-case number of binary-search probes inside the window, compared with binary search over all 12 keys?
options: 1 probe versus 12
3 probes versus 4
6 probes versus 12
2 probes versus 3
blocks.explain: The window holds 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 slots. Binary search over n slots needs at most floor(log2 n) + 1 probes: 3 for 6 slots and 4 for 12. Probe counts scale with the log of the window, which is why shrinking error from thousands to tens matters more than shrinking it from 6 to 3.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: to save build time, a team computes each leaf's min and max error on a 10% random sample of its keys, then searches only that window at lookup time.
options: Nothing breaks; sampling only makes the bounds slightly loose
Lookups get slower but always remain correct
Some stored keys can fall outside the window and lookups for them will wrongly report not found
The routing in stage 0 stops working
blocks.explain: The guarantee comes from checking every stored key. A key outside the sample can have a larger error than any sampled key, so a search limited to the window misses it. Either compute bounds on all keys (one pass, cheap) or search outward with exponential search, which needs no bounds.

lessons.title: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady

blocks.md:
A content delivery network (CDN) caches web and video objects close to users. Every miss is fetched across the wide-area network (WAN), and the CDN pays for those bytes, so the metric that matters is the **byte miss ratio**: the fraction of requested bytes not served from cache.

The LRB paper cites prior measurements that about 75% of CDN objects get no second request within two days (**one-hit wonders**). That is why major CDNs deploy **B-LRU**: LRU eviction plus a Bloom filter (a compact bit array that remembers, with rare false positives, which objects were seen before) so an object is admitted only on its second request, keeping one-hit wonders out. Even so, MIN beats it by 25 to 40% on their traces.

The obvious ML approach fails. To imitate MIN you would predict the next-request time of *every* cached object on every eviction (millions of predictions) and get the ranking of the very farthest one right. LRB changes the target instead.

**Relaxed Belady**: pick a threshold. On an eviction, split cached objects into set 1 (next request sooner than the threshold) and set 2 (at or beyond it). Evict any object from set 2, at random; only if set 2 is empty fall back to MIN within set 1. The **Belady boundary** is the threshold LRB uses: the smallest time-to-next-request among all objects MIN evicted during a warmup period.

blocks.title: Belady boundary and good decisions on the 12-request trace

scenes.caption: Lesson 1's trace with a 3-slot cache. MIN made 4 evictions. The bottom row shows, for each evicted object, how many requests later it was needed again.
The Belady boundary is the smallest of those distances: min(6, 4, never, never) = 4 requests. MIN never evicted anything needed sooner than that.
Now grade LRU's 7 evictions against the boundary. An eviction is good if the object is not needed for at least 4 requests. Evicting A at request 3 is bad: A returns 1 request later.
All 7 graded: 4 good, 3 bad, a good decision ratio of 4/7 = 57%. MIN scores 4/4 by construction. Each decision is judged on its own, without rerunning the whole cache.

blocks.md: The **good decision ratio** (good evictions divided by all evictions) grades each eviction individually. The LRB authors found it correlates strongly with the final byte miss ratio, so they used it to choose features, model, loss and sizes from one simulation pass instead of hours-long full simulations per design.

Relaxing costs something. On the Wikipedia trace, relaxed Belady with the boundary as threshold had 9 to 13% more misses than MIN across 64 GB to 1 TB caches, much smaller than the 25 to 40% gap to existing heuristics. In return, at a 64 GB cache about 19% of cached objects sat beyond the boundary, so a small random sample almost always contains a legal good eviction.

blocks.title: Chance that k random candidates include a set-2 object

scenes.caption: With p = 0.19 (Wikipedia, 64 GB), 4 random candidates contain a set-2 object with probability 0.570; 16 candidates, 0.966; 64 candidates, 0.9999986.
With p = 0.10, 64 candidates still give 0.9988. Simplified model: candidates are independent and the model must still recognize which one is beyond the boundary.
Even at p = 0.02, 64 candidates give 0.726. Sampling turns an impossible ranking problem (find the single farthest) into an easy one (find any far one among 64).

blocks.md:
**Features.** LRB keeps, for each object requested within a sliding **memory window**:

- **Deltas**: $\Delta_1$ is the time since the last request, $\Delta_2$ the gap between the two before that, up to 32 deltas. LRU uses only $\Delta_1$; LRU-K effectively uses the sum of $\Delta_1$ to $\Delta_k$.
- **Exponentially decayed counters** (EDCs): 10 request counts that forget at different speeds.
- **Static features**: object size and type (for example a live video segment versus video on demand).

blocks.caption: Updated on each request to the object. C_i halves after 2 to the power (9+i) requests of idleness: 1,024 for C_1 and 524,288 for C_10. Time is counted in requests.

blocks.title: EDCs of one object requested at t = 0, 1000, 1500, 1600

scenes.caption: First request: every counter starts at 0 and becomes 1.
Second request after 1,000 idle requests. EDC 1 has decayed almost by half before adding 1 (1.508); EDC 10 barely decayed (1.999).
Third request, 500 later: 2.075, 2.918, 2.997.
Fourth, 100 later: 2.939, 3.905, 3.997. The slow counter approximates a plain count; the fast one weighs recent bursts. Together they describe popularity over several horizons.

blocks.md:
**Model and labels.** LRB trains a gradient boosting machine (GBM, via LightGBM) with L2 loss to predict $\log$(time to next request). The log matters because only the side of the boundary matters: with a boundary of 1M requests, confusing 100K with 2M is far worse than confusing 2M with 3M.

Training data is sampled over **objects**, not requests, so popular objects do not drown out the cold ones the model must learn to evict. A sample is labeled when the object is requested again, or, if it leaves the memory window first, labeled 2 times the window size, which is safely beyond the boundary.

blocks.title: LRB's online loop (after Figure 7 of the paper)

scenes.caption: Every request updates the object's deltas and EDCs inside the sliding memory window, whose length LRB tunes to approximate the Belady boundary.
In the background, objects are sampled and later labeled. Once 128K labeled examples exist, a new GBM is trained (about 300 ms in the paper) and replaces the old one.
On a miss that needs space, LRB draws 64 random cached objects and predicts all of them in one batch, which the paper measured at about 30 microseconds.
It evicts the candidate with the farthest predicted next request. A wrong prediction only evicts a slightly worse object; correctness never depends on the model.

blocks.md: **Results.** In simulation on 6 production CDN traces, LRB cut WAN traffic by 4 to 25% versus B-LRU. The prototype inside Apache Traffic Server (ATS), replaying the Wikipedia trace on a 1 TB cache, reduced average WAN bandwidth by 44% and 95th-percentile bandwidth by 43%. At peak load it served 11.72 Gbps versus 11.66 for ATS, with peak CPU 16% versus 9%. Replayed at the trace's original speed, the object miss ratio fell from 5.7% to 2.6%.

blocks.question: LRB samples training examples uniformly over objects in the memory window rather than over requests. Why?
options: Sampling requests would be too slow to compute
Sampling requests over-represents popular objects, while the decisions LRB must learn are mostly about rarely requested objects it should evict
GBMs cannot train on duplicate objects
Objects that are never requested again would be sampled too often
blocks.explain: Per-request sampling picks a hot object once per request, so the dataset fills with objects that should obviously stay. The good evictions, objects beyond the boundary including those never requested again, would be rare. The paper samples over objects so both kinds are represented.

blocks.question: The boundary is 1M requests. Which training target choice best fits what LRB needs to get right?
options: log(time to next request), so the error between 100K and 2M counts more than between 2M and 3M
Raw time to next request with L2 loss, so large values dominate the loss
A binary label, recently used or not
The number of past requests
blocks.explain: The model only has to decide which side of the boundary an object falls on and rank the candidates. On a log scale a 20x error near the boundary is large while a 1.5x error far beyond it is small. The paper tried raw time, binary classification and other targets; log time gave the highest good decision ratio.

lessons.title: Decima: learning a cluster scheduler with reinforcement learning

blocks.md:
A Spark job is a **DAG** (directed acyclic graph) of **stages**. Each stage runs the same code over many data shards, one **task** per shard, and becomes runnable once all its parent stages finish. Tasks run on **executors** (worker slots). The scheduler repeatedly decides which runnable stage gets a free executor and how many executors each job may hold (its **parallelism**).

Common policies are simple: FIFO (first come, first served), shortest job first (SJF) and fair sharing. They ignore the DAG's shape and how well each job scales, both of which a scheduler could exploit.

The objective in Decima's main experiments is **average job completion time** (JCT): the mean over jobs of finish time minus arrival time. A tiny example shows how much the order alone matters: 3 jobs arrive at time 0 with 6, 2 and 4 one-second tasks, and there are 2 executors.

scenes.caption: FIFO runs J1, J2, J3 in arrival order. Finish times 3, 4 and 6 s: average JCT 13/3 = 4.33 s.
SJF runs the job with the least remaining work first: J2 finishes at 1, J3 at 3, J1 at 6. Average JCT 10/3 = 3.33 s, with the same total work and makespan.
Round-robin fair sharing interleaves jobs: J2 at 3, J3 at 5, J1 at 6. Average 14/3 = 4.67 s, worst of the three here. Simplified: equal 1 s tasks, no DAGs, perfect scaling.

blocks.md: In this toy SJF is optimal. Real jobs break that: stages depend on each other, tasks differ in length, and a job given 50 executors may not run much faster than with 20. On a 50-slot Spark cluster running 10 random TPC-H queries, Decima's paper shows SJF losing to fair sharing because it piles every slot onto one job past the point where extra parallelism helps.

blocks.title: Average JCT of 10 TPC-H jobs on 50 task slots (paper, Figure 3)

scenes.caption: Heuristics: FIFO 111.4 s, SJF 81.7 s, fair 74.9 s.
Decima 61.1 s: 45% lower than FIFO and about 18% lower than fair (the paper reports 19%). It finishes short jobs early but keeps each job near its parallelism sweet spot.

blocks.md: **State: a graph neural network.** Job DAGs have arbitrary shapes and sizes, so Decima cannot use a fixed-size input vector. Each stage $v$ has a feature vector $x_v$ (for example the number of remaining tasks and the expected task duration). A graph neural network passes messages from child stages up to parents, starting at the leaves, and reuses the same two small networks $f$ and $g$ at every node:

blocks.caption: xi(v) is the set of v's children. The paper found the outer non-linearity g critical: without it the network cannot express a max over children, which quantities like the critical path need.

blocks.title: Message passing computes a critical-path-like summary

scenes.caption: A 4-stage job: S1 runs first, then S2 and S3, then S4. Arrows point the way messages travel, from children back to parents. Work is total task-seconds per stage.
Step 1: leaf S4 has no children, so its summary is its own work. As a critical path (longest remaining chain), cp(S4) = 3.
Step 2: S2 and S3 receive S4's message. cp(S2) = 2 + 3 = 5 and cp(S3) = 6 + 3 = 9.
Step 3: S1 takes the max over its children: cp(S1) = 4 + max(5, 9) = 13. A sum (f and g as identity) would give a different, less useful number, which is why g matters.

Decima also adds a summary node per job and one global summary, computed with the same kind of update. The learned embeddings are vectors, not hand-defined values like cp; this example only shows what they can express.

blocks.md: **Actions.** At each scheduling event (a stage runs out of tasks, a stage completes, or a job arrives), a policy network scores every runnable stage from its node, job and global embeddings and samples one through a softmax. It also picks a **parallelism limit** for that stage's job; executors are assigned up to that limit, and the agent is called again while free executors remain. Splitting the decision this way keeps the action space small without needing very long action sequences.

**Reward.** After action $k$ at time $t_k$, the agent receives $r_k = -(t_k - t_{k-1}) J_k$, where $J_k$ is the number of jobs in the system during that interval. Summed over an episode this is minus the area under the jobs-in-system curve, and by Little's law (average jobs in system equals arrival rate times average time each job spends there) minimizing the time-average number of jobs minimizes average JCT.

blocks.prompt: In the SJF schedule above, the jobs-in-system count is 3 during [0, 1), 2 during [1, 3) and 1 during [3, 6). What is the total reward?
blocks.reveal: $-(1 \cdot 3) - (2 \cdot 2) - (3 \cdot 1) = -10$, exactly minus the sum of the three JCTs (1 + 3 + 6). FIFO earns -13 and fair earns -14, so the reward ranks the schedules the same way average JCT does.

blocks.md: **Training.** Decima learns in a simulator with **REINFORCE**, a policy gradient method: raise the log-probability of each action in proportion to how much better than expected the rewards after it turned out.

blocks.caption: pi_theta is the policy, alpha the learning rate and b_k a baseline that reduces the variance of the gradient estimate.

blocks.md:
Two problems are specific to scheduling with continuous random job arrivals:

- **Random arrivals add noise.** A burst of big jobs makes every action look bad, though the action did not cause it. Decima replays the same arrival sequence in several episodes and computes the baseline $b_k$ only over episodes with that same sequence (an input-dependent baseline).
- **Early policies are terrible**, and queues explode in long episodes. Episodes are cut short early in training and lengthened gradually (a curriculum). The cutoff time is random (memoryless); with a fixed cutoff the agent learns to delay large jobs until the episode ends.

**Results.** In batch experiments (20 unseen TPC-H jobs) Decima cut average JCT by 21% versus the best tuned heuristic, a weighted fair policy. With continuous arrivals it was 29% lower, and about 2 times faster during the busiest hours. Scheduling decisions took under 15 ms on average, while events typically arrived seconds apart.

A learned policy optimizes exactly the setting it was trained in. Decima trained on batched arrivals learned to defer large jobs, which minimizes the sum of JCTs for a fixed batch. Under continuous arrivals that starves large jobs, and it fell behind the tuned weighted fair heuristic at cluster loads above 65%.

blocks.question: Why does Decima end training episodes at a random, memoryless time instead of a fixed horizon?
options: Random cutoffs make the simulator faster
With a fixed horizon, the agent can learn to postpone large jobs until just before the episode ends, a strategy that fails in a real cluster that never stops
REINFORCE requires episodes of random length to converge
Fixed horizons cause the graph neural network to overflow
blocks.explain: If the end is predictable, delaying large jobs past it hides their cost from the reward. A memoryless cutoff gives no time at which deferring work becomes free, so the agent has to schedule as if the cluster runs forever.

blocks.question: Two training episodes use the same policy and the same actions early on, but in one a burst of 50 large jobs arrives at minute 5. What problem does this cause for policy gradient, and what fixes it?
options: The policy network runs out of memory; batch smaller
The reward becomes positive; clip it
The GNN cannot handle 50 DAGs; cap the number of jobs
Rewards differ for reasons unrelated to the action, inflating gradient variance; compare each episode against a baseline computed from episodes with the same arrival sequence
blocks.explain: The burst lowers every later reward regardless of what the agent did, so the advantage term blames or credits actions for luck. Decima's input-dependent baseline averages only over episodes that saw the same job arrivals, removing that noise from the comparison.

lessons.title: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails

blocks.md: The three systems teach the same engineering lessons. A learned component must fit an **inference budget** on the decision path, must be **retrained** as the workload moves, and must **fail soft** when its predictions are wrong. Each paper pays these costs in a different way.

**Inference budget.** Compare the cost of one decision with how often decisions happen:

- Learned index: a lookup must beat a roughly 300 ns B-tree traversal, so the model is a few multiply-adds in generated C++, not a framework call (80,000 ns in the paper's naive version).
- LRB: one batch prediction over 64 candidates takes about 30 microseconds, paid only on evictions, which the prototype made asynchronous through a lock-free admission queue.
- Decima: under 15 ms per decision on average, against events that typically arrive seconds apart.

blocks.prompt: A cache server evicts 10,000 objects per second and each eviction runs a 30 microsecond model. What fraction of one CPU core goes to inference?
blocks.reveal: 10,000 times 30 microseconds is 0.3 core-seconds every second, so **30% of one core**. That is why LRB samples only 64 candidates instead of scoring the whole cache, and why its authors first checked that their CDN servers had spare CPU (Wikipedia's CDN peaked below 30% CPU load in their measurements).

blocks.title: Where each system puts its guardrail

scenes.caption: Learned index: the search is limited to the stored error window, and leaves with too large an error become B-trees. A bad model costs extra probes, never a wrong answer for a stored key.
LRB: the model only ranks a random sample of cached objects. Any eviction is legal, and with about 19% of objects beyond the boundary, most samples hold a good choice.
Decima: the policy chooses only among runnable stages, and each action must add at least one executor, so every action sequence ends and yields a valid schedule.
Common shape: the model decides inside a space the system already knows is safe. Quality depends on the model; correctness does not.

blocks.md: Guardrails can also be proven. **Learning-augmented algorithms** treat the model as an untrusted oracle. Lykouris and Vassilvitskii show for caching that naively following an oracle's eviction advice can perform very poorly even when its average error is low. Their modified Marker algorithm has a competitive ratio (worst-case cost relative to the offline optimum) that shrinks as the oracle's error shrinks, yet is always capped at $O(\log k)$ for a cache of size $k$, the guarantee achievable with no oracle at all.

Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

**Drift.** Workloads change. LRB retrains continuously: each time 128K new labeled examples accumulate it trains a fresh model and swaps it in, so the model tracks recent traffic. Decima trains offline, so it depends on how closely training workloads match the real one. The paper tests this by training on different job interarrival times and testing on a 45-second interarrival workload.

blocks.title: Decima under workload shift: average JCT (paper, Table 2)

scenes.caption: Baseline: the tuned weighted fair heuristic averages 91.2 s. Decima trained on the same 45 s interarrival time (IAT) as the test workload: 65.4 s.
Trained on a mismatched 75 s IAT, Decima averages 104.8 s, 15% worse than the heuristic. The learned policy encoded the wrong arrival pattern.
Training on a mix of IATs recovers a 10% gain (82.3 s); also feeding the IAT as an input feature gives 16% (76.6 s). Diverse training data and features that describe the workload buy robustness.

blocks.md:
A practical checklist for applying ML to a systems policy:

1. **A measurable objective** and an offline yardstick (MIN, the best tuned heuristic) to know the headroom.
2. **Decisions that are frequent and individually cheap to get wrong**, with logged outcomes to learn from.
3. **A model that fits the budget**: linear models and GBMs on CPUs are often the right size; LRB found GBMs beat a small neural net for its tabular features.
4. **A guard** that keeps every decision legal, plus a fallback when the model is missing, stale or slow.
5. **A retraining plan** and a test against shifted workloads before trusting the gains.

Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

blocks.question: A team adds a learned eviction model to a key-value cache. In testing it cuts misses by 20%, but after a product launch shifts the traffic, misses are 30% above LRU. Which design change most directly limits this kind of damage?
options: Use a larger neural network so it generalizes better
Retrain on recent traffic continuously and track the miss ratio of a shadow LRU, switching back when the model loses
Score every object in the cache instead of a sample
Stop logging outcomes to save memory
blocks.explain: The failure is drift. Continuous retraining (as LRB does every 128K examples) tracks the new traffic, and comparing against a cheap shadow heuristic gives a fallback with a bounded loss. A bigger model trained on the old data still encodes the old workload.

blocks.question: Which statement about learned indexes, LRB and Decima is correct?
options: All three need the model to be correct to return correct results
None of them needs retraining once deployed
In all three, the model chooses among options the system already guarantees are valid, so mistakes cost performance rather than correctness
All three use deep neural networks at decision time
blocks.explain: The index searches a verified window (or a B-tree leaf), LRB evicts some cached object, and Decima only schedules runnable stages. Model quality changes speed or miss ratio. LRB uses GBMs and the index uses mostly linear leaves, and both indexes and caches need retraining as data changes.

blocks.question: Using Lykouris and Vassilvitskii's result, what happens to their predictor-augmented Marker algorithm if the oracle's predictions become arbitrarily bad?
options: It stays within O(log k) of optimal, the same bound as classic Marker without predictions
Its competitive ratio grows without bound
It becomes exactly as good as Belady's MIN
It refuses to evict
blocks.explain: The point of the construction is robustness: the ratio improves as prediction error falls, but it is always capped by O(log k), which is achievable with no oracle at all. Blindly following the oracle has no such cap.
